pages.text: Aseda and her cousin Eku paddled across Lake Tadane in the Western Region. Ahead stood Nzulezo, a whole village built on stilts above the water. Its name, in the Nzema language, means “surface of water.” “It looks as though the houses are floating,” said Aseda.
sentences: Aseda and her cousin Eku paddled across Lake Tadane in the Western Region.
Ahead stood Nzulezo, a whole village built on stilts above the water.
Its name, in the Nzema language, means “surface of water.” “It looks as though the houses are floating,” said Aseda.
pages.alt: Two children paddle a canoe toward a village on stilts over a lake.

pages.text: In Nzulezo, everyday life happens on the lake: cooking, school, worship and visiting neighbours by canoe or along wooden walkways. Opanin Eshun, an elder, welcomed them. “We are glad you came with respect,” he said. “Please ask before taking photographs.”
sentences: In Nzulezo, everyday life happens on the lake: cooking, school, worship and visiting neighbours by canoe or along wooden walkways.
Opanin Eshun, an elder, welcomed them.
“We are glad you came with respect,” he said.
“Please ask before taking photographs.”
pages.alt: An elder greets the children on a wooden walkway between stilt houses.

pages.text: “Tell us how our village began,” said Eku. Opanin Eshun smiled. “Our people say our ancestors came long ago from a city called Walata, in the old Ghana empire. They were seeking a safe home. A snail led them across the land to this lake. They settled where the snail stopped, and so a snail is part of our story.”
sentences: “Tell us how our village began,” said Eku.
Opanin Eshun smiled.
“Our people say our ancestors came long ago from a city called Walata, in the old Ghana empire.
They were seeking a safe home.
A snail led them across the land to this lake.
They settled where the snail stopped, and so a snail is part of our story.”
pages.alt: A big snail leads a line of travellers toward a lake.

pages.text: “How long ago?” asked Aseda. “About four hundred years, we say.” “Is that written down?” asked Eku. “Our story is carried by people, from grandparents to grandchildren,” said Opanin Eshun. “We call that oral history. It is a valuable record.” Aseda wrote: Oral history = history told from person to person.
sentences: “How long ago?” asked Aseda.
“About four hundred years, we say.” “Is that written down?” asked Eku.
“Our story is carried by people, from grandparents to grandchildren,” said Opanin Eshun.
“We call that oral history.
It is a valuable record.” Aseda wrote: Oral history = history told from person to person.
pages.alt: A grandfather tells a story to children sitting around him.

pages.text: “So is there a mystery?” asked Eku. “A historian might ask: how can we check an oral story?” said Opanin Eshun. “Written records, archaeology, languages and other communities’ stories can help. A story that fits many kinds of evidence becomes stronger. A story that we cannot yet check is not false. It is open.”
sentences: “So is there a mystery?” asked Eku.
“A historian might ask: how can we check an oral story?” said Opanin Eshun.
“Written records, archaeology, languages and other communities’ stories can help.
A story that fits many kinds of evidence becomes stronger.
A story that we cannot yet check is not false.
It is open.”
pages.alt: A historian compares an old map, a pot and a tale.

pages.text: “And why live on the water?” asked Aseda. “Our elders say it kept us safe, and the water brings fish and trade,” said Opanin Eshun. “It also taught us to care for the lake. We keep some days quiet. On Thursday, we avoid heavy work on the lake, as our ancestors taught us.” Eku nodded. “Respect again,” he said.

“It also taught us to care for the lake.
We keep some days quiet.
On Thursday, we avoid heavy work on the lake, as our ancestors taught us.” Eku nodded.
“Respect again,” he said.
pages.alt: Villagers rest on a quiet day with canoes tied to the walkway.

pages.text: Aseda thought about the mystery. “So we know the village is real,” she said. “We know the people tell a clear story. But historians still want more evidence about where exactly the ancestors came from and when.” “Yes,” said Opanin Eshun. “A good historian listens to elders and also looks for other clues.”

But historians still want more evidence about where exactly the ancestors came from and when.” “Yes,” said Opanin Eshun.
“A good historian listens to elders and also looks for other clues.”
pages.alt: The children and the elder talk on the walkway as the sun sets.

pages.text: Back home, Aseda and Eku made a poster: Nzulezo: What we know and what we honour. Known: a village on stilts, a lake, a living community. Told: the snail story. Open: how historians can check it. “Some mysteries,” said Aseda, “are not for solving. They are for learning from.” The end.
